t: #2231 Largest Number After Digit Swaps by Parity — Editorial
o:
Digits of the same parity can be freely permuted among themselves (adjacent transpositions generate all permutations of a parity class). Therefore the answer is obtained independently: sort the even digits descending into the even slots, and the odd digits descending into the odd slots.

For `1234`: odds `{1,3}` become `3,1`; evens `{2,4}` become `4,2`, giving `3412`. For `65875`: odds `{5,7,5}` → `7,5,5`; evens `{6,8}` → `8,6`, giving `87655`.

`num ≤ 10⁹` means at most 10 digits, so sorting is trivial.
k: Same-parity digits are mutually interchangeable, so slot parity is preserved under any swap sequence.
To maximize the number, put the largest available digit of the required parity in each position, left to right.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort Each Parity Class Descending
a.i: Extract digits, bucket by parity, sort each bucket in descending order, then rebuild the number filling each original parity slot with the next largest digit of that parity.
s: Split digits into even and odd lists; sort both descending.
Walk the original digit string; for each position take the next digit from the matching sorted bucket.
Parse the result back to an integer.
a.t: O(d log d) where d ≤ 10 is the number of digits — sorting tiny buckets dominates.

w: This is the natural and optimal approach; a heap per parity achieves the same thing. Pitfall: remember parity is preserved per position, so you cannot simply sort all digits. No meaningful follow-ups beyond handling leading zeros (impossible here since num ≥ 1).
